problems.title: Abelian subgroup covers
problems.summary: How many abelian subgroups are needed to cover a group with a bounded pairwise-noncommuting set?
problems.question: Write a(G) for the minimum abelian-subgroup cover size and omega(G) for the maximum pairwise-noncommuting set size. The global function h(n) takes the supremum over ALL groups with omega(G) <= n.
problems.boundary: The graph-family formula has an ordinary proof. Lean checks both binary map optima. The group realization and general finite-field extension have separate written arguments. Lecomte’s November preprint claims the unrestricted profile.
problems.next_question: Can a three-output alternating map on five binary coordinates outside the graphical family have a strict gap between its cover and clique numbers?
problems.falsifier: Exhibit such a nongraphical map and certify its two optima independently, or exhaust the precisely defined class.

results.title: Coupled-padding rank budget
results.scope: Two restriction-rank inequalities; regression is finite, not a global cover theorem.

results.title: Central-basis shear counterexample
results.scope: A named scalar rank can change without changing commutation.

results.title: Basis-invariant cross-radical bound
results.scope: A clique lower bound over the scalar-form space; no new global h(n) bound.

results.title: Two groups of order 64
results.scope: Matching clique and cover witnesses of sizes 9 and 5. The associated small Lean predicates are separate from this group-level proof.

results.title: 4,096 ordered form pairs
results.scope: Complete stated two-coordinate family on F2^4; not all groups of order 64.

results.title: 2,825 rank-four kernels
results.scope: All alternating commutation geometries on F2^4; equality of clique and isotropic-cover numbers in that domain.

results.title: 174,251 rank-five scalar planes
results.scope: The two-coordinate F2^5 class; three-coordinate cases are outside this census.

results.title: Binary graph covers equal the number of dominating supports
results.scope: For each finite simple Boolean graph, the binary edge alternating map admits a clique of all dominating supports and a matching cover by isotropic subspaces. Both optimization inequalities hold over all binary vectors. This entry concerns the map theorem.

results.title: Exact graphical clique and cover numbers over finite fields
results.scope: For edge commutator maps on a finite simple graph over any finite field, a weighted sum over dominating supports counts both optima and the maximal isotropic subspaces. The written proof also treats the associated graphical groups. Two independent odd-field examples exercise the construction.

problems.title: Sparse rulers and difference bases
problems.summary: Find small sets of marks whose differences cover every required distance.
problems.question: For a ruler on {0,...,N}, every distance 1,...,N must occur as a difference of two marks. The original experiment suite remains in the repository root.
problems.boundary: The current stability theorem concerns a fixed-length two-deletion, one-insertion edit on the canonical Wichmann family. The unrestricted sparse-ruler asymptotic optimum is a different question.
problems.next_question: Does every legal two-delete, one-insert edit of the canonical ruler miss at least r+5 distances for every r ≥ 2?
problems.falsifier: Find one r ≥ 33 and an explicit permitted edit missing at most r+4 distances. The two-junction construction gives the matching upper bound for every r ≥ 2.

results.title: Prior baseline for a strict middle and exterior deletion
results.scope: Deleting one strict middle mark and one exterior mark and adding one fresh integer cannot keep full distance coverage in W(r,2r). This result and its collision table were available before the duel and earned zero match points.

results.title: No perfect two-delete, one-insert repair
results.scope: At the original length of W(r,2r), every two original deletions and one fresh insertion miss a positive distance for r ≥ 1. The proof combines unique-distance and residue counts with a finite boundary checked independently through r=16. Lean verifies the residue lemmas.

results.title: Two-junction edit misses exactly r+5 distances
results.scope: Delete the junctions L and R and insert L+b. The exact complementary set has cardinality r+5 for every r ≥ 2. Literal pair enumeration checks the full set through radius 100. This is an upper bound on the minimum across edits.

results.title: The best repair deficit divided by r tends to one
results.scope: For every r ≥ 2, the minimum number of missing distances in the full edit domain is between max(1,r−8) and r+5. The written argument proves the geometry. Lean proves specific modular lemmas and the rational epsilon implication assuming those inequalities.

results.title: Exact repair minima at 32 radii and eight held-out predictions
results.scope: Metal and independent C++ enumerated 213,936 deletion pairs and 1,657,494,000 legal edit triples at fixed length. The optimum is 4 at radius 1 and r+5 for radii 2 through 32. The prediction for 25 through 32 was committed before evaluation.

problems.title: Modular distinct subset sums
problems.summary: Understand the structure of n-element sets with all subset sums distinct modulo 2^n+5.
problems.question: Compare admissible sets with signed unit dilations of {1,2,4,...,2^(n-1)}. This is a separately tracked research branch; no unverified Erdős problem number is assigned.
problems.boundary: The certified n=6 result is not a proof for every n. Sign reduction, completeness and the independent checker are part of the finite claim.
problems.next_question: At n=7 and modulus 133, can an admissible set require more than one replacement to reach a signed, unit-scaled powers-of-two set?
problems.falsifier: One fully verified set at replacement distance at least two refutes the proposed all-n pattern. An incomplete search with no counterexample does not prove it.

results.title: Modulus 69: complete n=6 case
results.scope: 4,224 admissible sets; each is within one replacement of signed unit-scaled powers of two. No all-n theorem.
